description: CELESTIAL PIRATES WE'RE HERE TO DOMINATE
summary:
BurnBridge is an interactive Earth observation platform that makes NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS fire records easier to explore, compare, and understand. We developed a web application featuring a 25-year burning calendar, geographic heatmaps, a synchronized 3D globe, observation logs, seasonal indicators, backtesting results, and downloadable JSON reports. The MVP uses original NASA FIRMS observations from five regions: Punjab, Kalimantan, California, the Amazon Basin, and Boreal Canada.

The project addresses a key challenge: MODIS and VIIRS observe fires at different resolutions, sensitivities, and times. Simply merging their hotspot counts can create misleading trends. BurnBridge places detections on a shared spatial grid and counts distinct observed fire-days, reducing duplicate counting while preserving each sensor’s record. Users can inspect differences, compare seasonal patterns, and review measured performance. Missing observations remain unknown, and source metadata makes results traceable. Validated cross-sensor calibration remains a future step.

BurnBridge matters because reliable interpretation of fire history requires understanding both environmental change and satellite sampling differences. By turning complex observations into accessible maps and transparent evidence, it helps researchers, students, and communities investigate burning patterns and understand the strengths and limitations of satellite fire monitoring.
details:
BurnBridge is a web platform for exploring NASA’s historical fire observations and understanding the differences between MODIS and VIIRS. Our working MVP combines an interactive map, a synchronized 3D globe, a year-by-year burning calendar, sensor comparisons, observation logs, and seasonal analysis. It currently includes original NASA FIRMS data for Punjab, Kalimantan, California, the Amazon Basin, and Boreal Canada.

How it works

Our Python pipeline downloads NASA FIRMS standard-processing archives, filters detections by location and confidence, and prepares JSON datasets. It organizes observations into a common 0.1° geographic grid. Within each sensor family, multiple detections in the same cell on the same day count as one observed fire-day. This reduces duplicate counting while preserving differences between MODIS and VIIRS.

Users select a region, instrument, year, and week, or draw a custom area. The calendar, geographic heatmap, globe, and indicators update together. Earth Lab replays recorded weekly activity, while the observation viewer exposes acquisition timestamps, satellite platforms, confidence values, and fire radiative power where available in the raw records.

The analysis includes annual sensor histories, comparisons of weeks with detections from both instruments, and seasonal baseline backtesting. The baseline uses only earlier years to estimate a later recorded week, allowing users to inspect measured prediction errors. A background-worker benchmark measures processing performance on actual records.

Benefits and intended impact

BurnBridge helps users recognize how instrument resolution, sensitivity, and sampling can influence apparent fire trends. Its visual interface supports education, exploratory research, and communication about seasonal burning. Simple mode presents accessible summaries; Expert mode adds provenance, diagnostics, and JSON exports.

Our intended impact is to make satellite fire evidence more understandable and reproducible, providing a foundation for future research into a consistent long-term fire record.

Tools and technologies

We developed the application using JavaScript, React, HTML, and CSS, with Vite for building and Vercel for deployment. Leaflet provides interactive mapping, Three.js renders the globe, and Recharts displays analytical charts. Python handles archive processing, while Web Workers keep benchmarks and country-data preparation responsive. We used Node.js tests and Playwright browser checks to verify calculations, navigation, synchronization, and mobile behavior. The application runs on ordinary computers and compatible mobile browsers without specialized hardware.

Creative approach and design considerations

Our creative contribution is connecting a 25-year weekly calendar to both geographic and globe-based views, then placing inspectable evidence beside those visualizations. Users can move from a historical pattern to its location, sensor record, and supporting source information within one workflow.

We considered scientific integrity, accessibility, browser performance, hosting cost, and reproducibility. Missing observations remain unknown because a missing hotspot can reflect cloud, sampling gaps, or unavailable data. Common-grid aggregation reduces duplicate counting but does not eliminate sensor bias. The MVP therefore presents observed activity and conditional comparisons transparently; validated harmonization, calibrated trust probabilities, and physical fire-spread forecasting remain future work.
